claim: The Journal Impact Factor (JIF) was originally developed to help libraries make indexing and purchasing decisions for their journal collections.
source: The Journal Impact Factor (JIF) was originally developed to help libraries make indexing and purchasing decisions for their journal collections (Garfield, 2006; Archambault and Larivière, 2009; Haustein and Larivière, 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by three citations to scholarly work (Garfield, 2006; Archambault and Larivière, 2009; Haustein and Larivière, 2015).

claim: Eugene Garfield, the JIF's creator, made it clear that the JIF was not appropriate for evaluating individuals or for assessing the significance of individual articles.
source: the metric's creator, Eugene Garfield, made it clear that the JIF was not appropriate for evaluating individuals or for assessing the significance of individual articles (Garfield, 1963)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Garfield's 1963 work.

claim: The JIF has various well-documented limitations.
source: the various well-documented limitations of the metric (e.g., Seglen, 1997; Moustafa, 2015; Brembs et al., 2013; The PLOS Medicine Editors, 2006; Kurmis, 2003; Sugimoto and Larivière, 2018; Haustein and Larivière, 2015; The Analogue University, 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to scholarly work documenting limitations.

claim: Over the past few decades the JIF has increasingly been used as a proxy measure to rank journals and, by extension, the articles and authors published in these journals.
source: over the past few decades the JIF has increasingly been used as a proxy measure to rank journals – and, by extension, the articles and authors published in these journals (Casadevall and Fang, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Casadevall and Fang, 2014.

claim: The association between the JIF, journal prestige, and selectivity is strong.
source: The association between the JIF, journal prestige, and selectivity is strong, and has led academics to covet publications in journals with high JIFs (Harley et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Harley et al., 2010.

claim: Academics covet publications in journals with high JIFs.
source: The association between the JIF, journal prestige, and selectivity is strong, and has led academics to covet publications in journals with high JIFs (Harley et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Harley et al., 2010.

claim: Publishers promote their JIF to attract academic authors.
source: Publishers, in turn, promote their JIF to attract academic authors (Hecht et al., 1998; Sugimoto and Larivière, 2018; SpringerNature, 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by three citations to scholarly work and publisher materials.

claim: In some academic disciplines, it is considered necessary to have publications in journals with high JIFs to succeed, especially for those on the tenure track.
source: In some academic disciplines, it is considered necessary to have publications in journals with high JIFs to succeed, especially for those on the tenure track (for review see Schimanski and Alperin, 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review by Schimanski and Alperin, 2018.

claim: Institutions in some countries financially reward their faculty for publishing in journals with high JIFs.
source: Institutions in some countries financially reward their faculty for publishing in journals with high JIFs (Fuyuno and Cyranoski, 2006; Quan et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by two citations to scholarly work.

claim: Faculty often report intense pressure to publish in journals with high JIFs.
source: Even when the incentives are not so clear-cut, faculty still often report intense pressure to publish in these venues (Harley et al., 2010; Walker et al., 2010; Tijdink et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by three citations to scholarly work.

claim: Concerns about the JIF and journals' perceived prestige may limit the adoption of open access publishing.
source: Concerns about the JIF and journals' perceived prestige may also limit the adoption of open access publishing (Schroter et al., 2005; Swan and Brown, 2004; University of California Libraries, 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by three citations to scholarly work and institutional reports.

claim: The use and potential misuse of the JIF to evaluate research and researchers is often raised in broader discussions about the many problems with current academic evaluation systems.
source: This use – and potential misuse – of the JIF to evaluate research and researchers is often raised in broader discussions about the many problems with current academic evaluation systems (Moher et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moher et al., 2018.

claim: The study collected documents related to the RPT process from a representative sample of universities in the United States and Canada.
source: This paper reports a set of findings from a larger study (Alperin et al., 2019) for which we collected documents related to the RPT process from a representative sample of universities in the United States and Canada and many of their academic units.
evidence: The authors describe their methodology, which is also documented in a cited larger study.

claim: The study created a stratified random sample based on the 2015 edition of the Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education and the 2016 edition of the Maclean's University Rankings.
source: we created a stratified random sample based on the 2015 edition of the Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education (Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching, 2015) and the 2016 edition of the Maclean's University Rankings (Rogers Digital Media, 2016)
evidence: The authors describe their sampling methodology with citations to the classification systems used.

claim: The study obtained 864 documents related to the RPT process of 129 universities.
source: In the end, we obtained 864 documents related to the RPT process of 129 universities, of which 57 were R-type, 39 were M-type, and 33 were B-type institutions.
evidence: The authors report the number of documents collected in their study.

claim: Of the total 864 documents, 370 were institutional-level documents, while the remaining 494 came from 381 academic units within 60 of these universities.
source: Of the total documents, 370 were institutional-level documents, while the remaining 494 came from 381 academic units within 60 of these universities.
evidence: The authors report the breakdown of documents by level in their study.

claim: The study classified terms found in RPT documents into three groups: direct references to the JIF as a metric, those that reference journal impact in some way, and indirect but possible references to the JIF.
source: We classified these terms into three groups: (1) direct references to the JIF as a metric; (2) those that reference journal impact in some way; and (3) indirect but possible references to the JIF.
evidence: The authors describe their classification methodology.

claim: The first group of terms includes 'impact factor', 'impact score', 'impact metric', and 'impact index'.
source: In the first group, we included the terms "impact factor", "impact score", "impact metric", and "impact index".
evidence: The authors explicitly list the terms in the first group.

claim: The second group of terms includes 'high-impact journal', 'impact of the journal', and 'journal('s) impact'.
source: In the second group, we included the terms "high-impact journal", "impact of the journal", and "journal('s) impact".
evidence: The authors explicitly list the terms in the second group.

claim: The study analyzed only the first two groups of terms, as they were considered to be unambiguously about the JIF or sufficiently close to the notion of JIF.
source: In our analysis, we looked at only the first two groups of terms, as we considered them to be unambiguously about the JIF (group 1) or sufficiently close to the notion of JIF (group 2).
evidence: The authors explain their analytical decision.

claim: Each of the JIF mentions was independently coded by two of the authors, and after an initial pass, the two coders agreed on all of the classifications for 86% of all mentions.
source: To arrive at the classification, each mention was independently coded by two of the authors (EM and LM) using the definitions above. After an initial pass, the two coders agreed on all of the classifications for 86% of all mentions.
evidence: The authors report their inter-coder reliability.

claim: The remaining mentions were independently coded by a third author, and in all instances, the third coder agreed with one of the previous two.
source: The remaining mentions were independently coded by a third author (LS). In all instances, the third coder agreed with one of the previous two, and this agreement was taken as the final code.
evidence: The authors describe their conflict resolution process for coding.

claim: Only 23% of institutions in the sample mentioned the JIF explicitly or used one of the JIF-related terms in their RPT documents.
source: While metrics in general are mentioned in RPT documents from 50% of institutions in our sample (Alperin et al., 2019), only 23% mentioned the JIF explicitly or used one of the JIF-related terms (see groups 1 and 2 in Figure 1) in their RPT documents.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on analysis of the collected documents.

claim: The percentage of institutions mentioning JIF-related terms was higher for R-type institutions (40%) than for either M-type (18%) or B-type (0%) institutions.
source: The percentage was higher for R-type institutions (40%) than for either M-type (18%) or B-type (0%) institutions (Table 2).
evidence: The authors report their finding based on analysis of the collected documents, with reference to Table 2.

claim: Within the R-type institutions, the percentage of academic units that mentioned JIF-related terms was higher for LS (33%) and PSM (29%) units than for SSH (21%) or multidisciplinary units (17%).
source: Within the R-type institutions, the percentage of academic units that mentioned JIF-related terms was higher for LS (33%) and PSM (29%) units than for SSH (21%) or multidisciplinary units (17%).
evidence: The authors report their finding based on analysis of the collected documents.

claim: 87% of institutions that mentioned the JIF did so supportively in at least one of their RPT documents.
source: Overall, 87% of institutions that mentioned the JIF did so supportively in at least one of their RPT documents from our sample (Table 2).
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents, with reference to Table 2.

claim: 83% of R-type institutions that mentioned the JIF had supportive mentions.
source: Breaking down by institution type, 83% of R-type and 100% of M-type institutions had supportive mentions.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: 100% of M-type institutions that mentioned the JIF had supportive mentions.
source: Breaking down by institution type, 83% of R-type and 100% of M-type institutions had supportive mentions.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: Just 13% of institutions overall had at least one mention which expressed caution about using the JIF in evaluations.
source: In contrast, just 13% of institutions overall had at least one mention which expressed caution about using the JIF in evaluations.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: Two institutions (University of Central Florida and University of Guelph) had both supportive and cautious mentions of the JIF, but originating from different academic units.
source: Two institutions (University of Central Florida and University of Guelph) had both supportive and cautious mentions of the JIF, but originating from different academic units.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: 17% of institutions had at least one neutral mention of the JIF.
source: Overall, 17% of institutions had at least one neutral mention.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: The most commonly specified association observed in RPT documents was between the JIF and quality, seen in 63% of institutions overall.
source: The most commonly specified association we observed in these RPT documents was between the JIF and quality, seen in 63% of institutions overall (Table 2).
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents, with reference to Table 2.

claim: 61% of R-type institutions that mention the JIF associate the metric with quality.
source: By institution type, 61% of R-type and 71% of M-type institutions in our sample that mention the JIF associate the metric with quality.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: 71% of M-type institutions that mention the JIF associate the metric with quality.
source: By institution type, 61% of R-type and 71% of M-type institutions in our sample that mention the JIF associate the metric with quality.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: The Faculty of Science at the University of Alberta states that impact factors and/or acceptance rates of refereed venues are useful measures of venue quality.
source: This association can be seen in the guidelines from the Faculty of Science at the University of Alberta that state: "Of all the criteria listed, the one used most extensively, and generally the most reliable, is the quality and quantity of published work in refereed venues of international stature. Impact factors and/or acceptance rates of refereed venues are useful measures of venue quality…" (University of Alberta, 2012).
evidence: The authors quote directly from the University of Alberta's RPT document.

claim: The Department of Political Science, International Development, and International Affairs at the University of Southern Mississippi considers journal impact factors as a measure of publication quality.
source: An example of the latter comes from the Department of Political Science, International Development, and International Affairs at the University of Southern Mississippi: "Consideration will be given to publication quality as measured by the following items (though not exclusive of other quality measures not listed here): journal/press rankings, journal/press reputation in the field, journal impact factors, journal acceptance rates, awards, citations, reviews and/or reprints" (University of Southern Mississippi, 2016).
evidence: The authors quote directly from the University of Southern Mississippi's RPT document.

claim: The Institute of Environmental Sustainability at Loyola University employs a metric that uses the JIF to calculate an Article Impact Factor, which they suggest will incentivize high quality research.
source: Other guidelines create their own metrics using the JIF in their calculations and suggest this will incentivize high quality research, as seen in the following example from the Institute of Environmental Sustainability at Loyola University: "For promotion to Professor, the candidate must have an average publication rate of at least one article per year published in peer-reviewed journals in the five-year period preceding the application for promotion. These articles should be regularly cited by other researchers in the field. We will consider both the quality of the journal (as measured by the journal's impact factor, or JIF) as well as the number of citations of each publication. We will employ the metric: Article Impact Factor (AIF) = (JIF * citations) where "citations" represents the number of citations for the particular publication. Employing this metric, faculty have incentive to publish in the highest quality journals (which will increase the JIF) and simultaneously produce the highest quality research manuscripts, potentially increasing the number of citations, and increasing the AIF" (Loyola University Chicago, 2015).
evidence: The authors quote directly from Loyola University's RPT document.

claim: The second most common specified association observed in RPT documents was between the JIF and the impact, importance, or significance of faculty research or publications, found in 40% of institutions in the sample.
source: The second most common specified association we observed in these RPT documents was between the JIF and the impact, importance, or significance of faculty research or publications, found in 40% of institutions in our sample.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: 35% of R-type institutions that mention the JIF associate it with impact, importance, or significance.
source: By institution type, 35% of R-type and 57% of M-type institutions made this association (Table 2).
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents, with reference to Table 2.

claim: 57% of M-type institutions that mention the JIF associate it with impact, importance, or significance.
source: By institution type, 35% of R-type and 57% of M-type institutions made this association (Table 2).
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents, with reference to Table 2.

claim: The Department of Psychology at Simon Fraser University considers impact factors as measures of the reach and impact of a candidate's scholarship.
source: For example, guidelines from the Department of Psychology at Simon Fraser University link the JIF with impact: "The TPC [Tenure and Promotion Committee] may additionally consider metrics such as citation figures, impact factors, or other such measures of the reach and impact of the candidate's scholarship" (Simon Fraser University, 2015).
evidence: The authors quote directly from Simon Fraser University's RPT document.

claim: The University of Windsor's promotion and tenure criteria link the JIF to publication importance.
source: Promotion and tenure criteria from the University of Windsor link the JIF to publication importance (University of Windsor, 2016): "Candidates will be encouraged to submit a statement that explains the importance of their publications, which may include factors such as journal impact factors, citation rates, publication in journals with low acceptance rates, high levels of readership, demonstrated importance to their field."
evidence: The authors quote directly from the University of Windsor's RPT document.

claim: The Department of History at the University of California, Los Angeles associates the JIF with significance of faculty work.
source: Guidelines from the Department of History at the University of California, Los Angeles associate the JIF with significance of faculty work: "The [policy on academic personnel]'s concern that the candidate be "continuously and effectively engaged in creative activity of high quality and significance," should further be demonstrated through other publications that include peer reviewed articles in high impact journals…".
evidence: The authors quote directly from UCLA's RPT document.

claim: 20% of institutions in the sample that mentioned the JIF associated the metric with prestige, reputation, or status.
source: A third set of mentions of the JIF associated the metric with prestige, reputation, or status, typically referring to the publication venue. Overall, 20% of institutions in our sample that mentioned the JIF made such an association.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: 22% of R-type institutions that mention the JIF associate it with prestige, reputation, or status.
source: As with other concepts, there was variability by institution type, with 22% of the R-type and 14% of the M-type having at least one instance of this association (Table 2).
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents, with reference to Table 2.

claim: 14% of M-type institutions that mention the JIF associate it with prestige, reputation, or status.
source: As with other concepts, there was variability by institution type, with 22% of the R-type and 14% of the M-type having at least one instance of this association (Table 2).
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents, with reference to Table 2.

claim: The Department of Sociology at the University of Central Florida links the JIF with journal prestige.
source: For example, guidelines from the Department of Sociology at the University of Central Florida link the JIF with prestige: "It is also true that some refereed journal outlets count for more than others. Publication in respected, highly cited journals, that is, counts for more than publication in unranked journals. The top journals in sociology and all other social sciences are ranked in the Thompson/ISI citation data base (which generates the well-known Impact Factors), in the Scopus data base, and in certain other citation data bases. In general, it behooves faculty to be aware of the prestige rankings of the field's journals and to publish in the highest-ranked journals possible. It is also advisable to include in one's tenure and promotion file information about the Impact Factors or related metrics for the journals where one's papers appear" (University of Central Florida, 2015).
evidence: The authors quote directly from the University of Central Florida's RPT document.

claim: The University of Vermont's promotion and tenure forms associate the JIF with journal status.
source: Similarly, promotion and tenure forms from the University of Vermont associate the JIF with journal status: "List all works reviewed prior to publication by peers/editorial boards in the field, such as journal articles in refereed journals, juried presentations, books, etc. Indicate up to five of the most important contributions with a double asterisk and briefly explain why these choices have been made. Include a description of the stature of journals and other scholarly venues and how this is known (e.g., impact factors, percentage of submitted work that is accepted, together with an explanation of the interpretation of these measures)" (University of Vermont, 2016).
evidence: The authors quote directly from the University of Vermont's RPT document.

claim: 77% of institutions that mentioned the JIF did so without specifying what it is intended to measure.
source: Such unspecified mentions were found in the RPT documents of 77% of institutions that mentioned the JIF.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: 74% of R-type institutions that mentioned the JIF did so without specifying what it is intended to measure.
source: These correspond to 74% of the R-type institutions and 86% of the M-type institutions with mentions (Table 2).
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents, with reference to Table 2.

claim: 86% of M-type institutions that mentioned the JIF did so without specifying what it is intended to measure.
source: These correspond to 74% of the R-type institutions and 86% of the M-type institutions with mentions (Table 2).
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents, with reference to Table 2.

claim: The Russ College of Engineering and Technology at Ohio University requests the JIF in their RPT guidelines.
source: For example, guidelines from the Russ College of Engineering and Technology at Ohio University request the JIF in the following way: "List relevant peer-reviewed journal and conference papers published over the last five years (or since last promotion or initial appointment, whichever is less) related to pedagogy or other relevant areas of education. Include the journal's impact factor (or equivalent journal ranking data) and the number of citations of the article(s)" (Ohio University, 2015).
evidence: The authors quote directly from Ohio University's RPT document.

claim: 13% of institutions had at least one mention which cautioned against or discouraged use of the JIF in evaluations.
source: While the majority of the mentions found in our sample of RPT documents were either neutral or supportive of the JIF, we find that 13% of institutions had at least one mention which cautioned against or discouraged use of the JIF in evaluations.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: The School of Social Work at the University of Central Florida states that journal impact factors will not be a primary criteria for the measurement of scholarly activity and prominence.
source: For example, criteria for promotion and tenure from the School of Social Work at the University of Central Florida state: "Journal impact factors will not be a primary criteria for the measurement of scholarly activity and prominence as the academic depth and breadth of the profession requires publication in a multitude of journals that may not have high impact factors, especially when compared to the stem [sic] disciplines" (University of Central Florida, 2014).
evidence: The authors quote directly from the University of Central Florida's RPT document.

claim: The Department of Human Health and Nutritional Sciences at the University of Guelph calls the JIF a 'problematic' index and discourages its use.
source: Similarly, guidelines from the Department of Human Health and Nutritional Sciences at the University of Guelph call the JIF a "problematic" index and discourage its use while again highlighting disciplinary differences: "Discussion of journal quality (by those familiar with the field) may be included in the assessment in addition to consideration of the quality of individual research contributions. However, citation analyses and impact factors are problematic indices, particularly in comparisons across fields, and their use in the review process is not encouraged" (University of Guelph, 2008).
evidence: The authors quote directly from the University of Guelph's RPT document.

claim: The Faculty of Veterinary Medicine at the University of Calgary cautions against relying solely on the JIF as a measure of quality, but still allows it to be considered.
source: Other guidelines, such as those from the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine at the University of Calgary, caution against relying solely on the JIF as a measure of quality, but still allow it to be considered: "Special consideration is to be given to the quality of the publication and the nature of the authorship. Contributions of the applicant must be clearly documented. The reputation and impact of the journal or other publication format will be considered, but takes secondary consideration to the quality of the publication and the nature of the contributions. Impact factors of journals should not be used as the sole or deciding criteria in assessing quality" (University of Calgary, 2008).
evidence: The authors quote directly from the University of Calgary's RPT document.

claim: A document from the Committee on Academic Personnel at the University of California, San Diego shows that some CAP members retain various degrees of skepticism about measures like the JIF.
source: Some RPT documents even seem to show disagreement within evaluation committees on the use of the JIF. For example, a document from the Committee on Academic Personnel at the University of California, San Diego reads: "CAP [Committee on Academic Personnel] welcomes data on journal acceptance rates and impact factors, citation rates and H-index, but some CAP members (as do senior staff of scholarly societies) retain various degrees of skepticism about such measures" (University of California, San Diego, 2016).
evidence: The authors quote directly from UC San Diego's RPT document.

claim: None of the RPT documents analyzed heavily criticize the JIF or prohibit its use in evaluations.
source: None of the RPT documents we analyzed heavily criticize the JIF or prohibit its use in evaluations.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: This is the first study of RPT documents from a representative sample of US and Canadian universities to analyze the use of the JIF in academic evaluations.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first study of RPT documents from a representative sample of US and Canadian universities to analyze the use of the JIF in academic evaluations.
evidence: The authors state this based on their knowledge of the literature.

claim: 40% of R-type institutions mentioned the JIF or related terms in their RPT documents.
source: We found that 40% of R-type and 18% of M-type institutions mentioned the JIF or related terms in their RPT documents.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on analysis of the collected documents.

claim: 18% of M-type institutions mentioned the JIF or related terms in their RPT documents.
source: We found that 40% of R-type and 18% of M-type institutions mentioned the JIF or related terms in their RPT documents.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on analysis of the collected documents.

claim: Mentions of the JIF in RPT documents were largely supportive of JIF use, with 87% of institutions having at least one supportive mention.
source: Mentions were largely supportive of JIF use, with 87% of institutions having at least one supportive mention, while just 13% had cautious mentions.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: Just 13% of institutions that mentioned the JIF had cautious mentions.
source: Mentions were largely supportive of JIF use, with 87% of institutions having at least one supportive mention, while just 13% had cautious mentions.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: The most common specified association observed in RPT documents was between the JIF and quality.
source: The most common specified association we observed in these documents was between the JIF and quality.
evidence: The authors report their finding based on qualitative analysis of the collected documents.

claim: The experiences at R-type universities (where mentions of the JIF were most prevalent) may play an outsized role in discussions about evaluation.
source: Importantly, we note that the results differ depending on institution type, which might suggest that the experiences at R-type universities (where mentions of the JIF were most prevalent) play an outsized role in discussions about evaluation.
evidence: The authors infer this from their findings about differential prevalence by institution type.

claim: Counting mentions of a restricted set of terms is likely an underestimate of the extent of the use of the JIF in RPT processes.
source: In short, counting mentions of a restricted set of terms, as we have done here, is likely an underestimate of the extent of the use of the JIF in RPT processes.
evidence: The authors infer this based on their observation of additional related terms not included in their analysis.

claim: Quality is hard to define, and even harder to measure.
source: Although quality is hard to define, and even harder to measure, there are aspects of methodological rigor which could be considered indicative of quality, such as sample size, experimental design, and reproducibility (Brembs, 2018).
evidence: The authors state this as general knowledge, with a citation to Brembs, 2018 for the aspects of methodological rigor.

claim: Aspects of methodological rigor which could be considered indicative of quality include sample size, experimental design, and reproducibility.
source: Although quality is hard to define, and even harder to measure, there are aspects of methodological rigor which could be considered indicative of quality, such as sample size, experimental design, and reproducibility (Brembs, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brembs, 2018.

claim: Fraley and Vazire (2014) found that social and personality psychology journals with the highest JIFs tend to publish studies with smaller sample sizes and lower statistical power.
source: For example, Fraley and Vazire (2014) found that social and personality psychology journals with the highest JIFs tend to publish studies with smaller sample sizes and lower statistical power.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fraley and Vazire, 2014.

claim: Munafò et al. (2009) report that higher-ranked journals tend to publish gene-association studies with lower sample sizes and overestimate effect sizes.
source: Similarly, Munafò et al. (2009) report that higher-ranked journals tend to publish gene-association studies with lower sample sizes and overestimate effect sizes.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Munafò et al., 2009.

claim: Analyses of neuroscience and/or psychology studies show either no correlation or a negative correlation between statistical power and the JIF.
source: Analyses of neuroscience and/or psychology studies show either no correlation (Brembs et al., 2013) or a negative correlation (Szucs and Ioannidis, 2017) between statistical power and the JIF.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brembs et al., 2013 and Szucs and Ioannidis, 2017.

claim: Chess and Gagnier (2013) found that less than 1% of clinical trial studies met all 10 quality criteria they analyzed.
source: Chess and Gagnier (2013) analyzed clinical trial studies for 10 different indicators of quality, including randomization and blinding, and found that less than 1% of studies met all 10 quality criteria, while the JIF of the journals did not significantly predict whether a larger number of quality criteria were met.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chess and Gagnier, 2013.

claim: Chess and Gagnier (2013) found that the JIF of the journals did not significantly predict whether a larger number of quality criteria were met.
source: Chess and Gagnier (2013) analyzed clinical trial studies for 10 different indicators of quality, including randomization and blinding, and found that less than 1% of studies met all 10 quality criteria, while the JIF of the journals did not significantly predict whether a larger number of quality criteria were met.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chess and Gagnier, 2013.

claim: Barbui et al. (2006) found no clear relationship between the JIF and study quality.
source: Barbui et al. (2006) used three different scales that take into account experimental design, bias, randomization, and more to assess quality, and found no clear relationship between the JIF and study quality.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barbui et al., 2006.

claim: Bustin et al. (2013) found a negative correlation between the JIF and the amount of methodological information provided in molecular biology studies.
source: Bustin et al. (2013) analyzed molecular biology studies and found key methodological details lacking, reporting a negative correlation between the JIF and the amount of information provided in the work.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bustin et al., 2013.

claim: Mobley et al. (2013) found that around half of biomedical researchers surveyed reported they were unable to reproduce a published finding, some from journals with a JIF over 20.
source: Mobley et al. (2013) found that around half of biomedical researchers surveyed reported they were unable to reproduce a published finding, some from journals with a JIF over 20.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mobley et al., 2013.

claim: Prinz et al. (2011) found that the reproducibility of published data did not significantly correlate with journal impact factors.
source: Prinz et al. (2011) found "that the reproducibility of published data did not significantly correlate with journal impact factors" (pg. 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Prinz et al., 2011.

claim: There is little to no evidence that the JIF measures research quality.
source: Thus, at least as viewed through the aspects above, there is little to no evidence that the JIF measures research quality. For a more comprehensive review, see Brembs (2018).
evidence: The authors conclude this based on the evidence they reviewed, with a citation to Brembs, 2018 for a comprehensive review.

claim: In the last few years, several proposals and initiatives have challenged the use of the JIF and promoted the responsible use of metrics to improve academic evaluations.
source: In the last few years, several proposals and initiatives have challenged the use of the JIF and promoted the responsible use of metrics to improve academic evaluations. These include the Leiden Manifesto (Hicks et al., 2015), the Metric Tide report (Wilsdon et al., 2015), the Next-Generation Metrics report (Wildson et al., 2017), and HuMetricsHSS (humetricshss.org).
evidence: The authors list several initiatives with citations and references.

claim: DORA outlines limitations of the JIF, and puts forward a general recommendation to not use the JIF in evaluations, especially as a 'surrogate measure of the quality of individual research articles'.
